evidence.claim: The official presidential biography records Jair Bolsonaro's term in office as 01/01/2019 to 31/12/2022.
evidence.title: Biografia
evidence.excerpt: The official presidential biography records Jair Bolsonaro's term in office as 01/01/2019 to 31/12/2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official government biography with explicit term dates.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Bolsonaro's office and term.
contrary_evidence: Biographical pages are favorable by design and omit controversy.

evidence.claim: Articles 83 and 84 assign the president executive authority, including appointing ministers, directing the federal administration, initiating legislation, promulgating laws, issuing decrees, and vetoing bills, while limiting foreign travel without congressional authorization.
evidence.title: Constituição da República Federativa do Brasil de 1988
evidence.excerpt: Articles 83 and 84 assign the president executive authority, including appointing ministers, directing the federal administration, initiating legislation, promulgating laws, issuing decrees, and vetoing bills, while limiting foreign travel without congressional authorization.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary constitutional text in force during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Defines Bolsonaro's formal authority and constraints in 2022.
contrary_evidence: Formal powers do not prove how they were used in practice.

evidence.claim: Brazil acceded to the NPT in 1998.
evidence.title: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons
evidence.excerpt: Brazil acceded to the NPT in 1998.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official UN depositary record for treaty accession.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Contextual baseline, not a Bolsonaro-specific initiative.
contrary_evidence: Accession is a formal commitment, not proof of implementation quality.

evidence.claim: Brazil ratified the Treaty of Tlatelolco, the Latin American nuclear-weapon-free-zone treaty, in 1968.
evidence.title: Treaty for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America
evidence.excerpt: Brazil ratified the Treaty of Tlatelolco, the Latin American nuclear-weapon-free-zone treaty, in 1968.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-level treaty posture, not personal authorship by Bolsonaro.
contrary_evidence: Treaty membership alone does not show active restraint in every year.

evidence.claim: Brazil appears in the treaty-status table as a signatory to the TPNW, with no ratification shown on the status page excerpt.
evidence.title: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons
evidence.excerpt: Brazil appears in the treaty-status table as a signatory to the TPNW, with no ratification shown on the status page excerpt.
evidence.period_fit: Status remained relevant in 2022 as an unratified signature.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-level treaty posture inherited by Bolsonaro.
contrary_evidence: A signature is weaker than ratification and does not by itself show operational policy change.

evidence.claim: Brazil's safeguards agreements include the Argentina-Brazil-IAEA quadripartite safeguards agreement and exchange-of-letters arrangements connected to the NPT and Tlatelolco framework.
evidence.title: Brazil, Federative Republic of
evidence.excerpt: Brazil's safeguards agreements include the Argentina-Brazil-IAEA quadripartite safeguards agreement and exchange-of-letters arrangements connected to the NPT and Tlatelolco framework.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional baseline rather than Bolsonaro-only action.
contrary_evidence: The page is legal status, not proof of day-to-day oversight quality.

evidence.claim: ABACC says its mission is to assure Brazil, Argentina, and the international community that nuclear materials and facilities are used exclusively for peaceful purposes and not diverted to nuclear weapons, and that the agency works with national authorities and the IAEA.
evidence.title: About
evidence.excerpt: ABACC says its mission is to assure Brazil, Argentina, and the international community that nuclear materials and facilities are used exclusively for peaceful purposes and not diverted to nuclear weapons, and that the agency works with national authorities and the IAEA.
evidence.source_locator: mission paragraphs on the About page
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official agency self-description of safeguards mission and coordination.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional safeguard environment, not direct Bolsonaro conduct.
contrary_evidence: Self-description is favorable and needs external corroboration for performance claims.

evidence.claim: The law created the Autoridade Nacional de Segurança Nuclear (ANSN) as an autonomous federal body responsible for monitoring, regulating, and inspecting nuclear safety, radiological protection, and physical security.
evidence.title: Lei nº 14.222, de 15 de outubro de 2021
evidence.excerpt: The law created the Autoridade Nacional de Segurança Nuclear (ANSN) as an autonomous federal body responsible for monitoring, regulating, and inspecting nuclear safety, radiological protection, and physical security.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary legal text establishing the regulator and its mandate.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant as the institutional framework in force during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Bolsonaro signed the law, so this is ruler-attributed institutional action.
contrary_evidence: Creation of a regulator is implementation, not proof of effective supervision in every case.

evidence.claim: The decree implemented ANSN's regimental structure and confirmed that it would monitor, regulate, and inspect nuclear safety, radiological protection, and physical security in Brazil.
evidence.title: Decreto nº 11.142, de 21 de julho de 2022
evidence.excerpt: The decree implemented ANSN's regimental structure and confirmed that it would monitor, regulate, and inspect nuclear safety, radiological protection, and physical security in Brazil.
contrary_evidence: This establishes structure, not performance or adequacy of enforcement.

evidence.claim: The decree promulgated the amendment to the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material and Nuclear Installations, a formal step toward stronger physical-security norms.
evidence.title: Decreto nº 11.188, de 5 de setembro de 2022
evidence.excerpt: The decree promulgated the amendment to the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material and Nuclear Installations, a formal step toward stronger physical-security norms.
evidence.source_locator: decree title and article 3 opening text
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary presidential decree implementing an international nuclear-security instrument.
contrary_evidence: Promulgation is formal compliance; it does not prove implementation quality at every facility.

evidence.claim: In 2022 ABACC reported a visit by CTBTO Executive Secretary Robert Floyd to exchange views on trust and confidence-building, and separate safeguards training for Brazil's Naval Agency for Nuclear Safety and Quality covering the legal basis of safeguards and inspection techniques.
evidence.title: News – ABACC
evidence.excerpt: In 2022 ABACC reported a visit by CTBTO Executive Secretary Robert Floyd to exchange views on trust and confidence-building, and separate safeguards training for Brazil's Naval Agency for Nuclear Safety and Quality covering the legal basis of safeguards and inspection techniques.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official institutional news page with dated 2022 activities.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional environment under Bolsonaro; not a personal Bolsonaro quote.
contrary_evidence: This is institutional process evidence, not proof of personal presidential initiative.

evidence.claim: Brazil's profile shows two nuclear power reactors in operation and one under construction, with nuclear power supplying a small share of electricity.
evidence.title: Country Nuclear Power Profiles - Brazil
evidence.publication_date: current profile with data as of 2026-07-08
evidence.excerpt: Brazil's profile shows two nuclear power reactors in operation and one under construction, with nuclear power supplying a small share of electricity.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official IAEA reactor and country-profile data.
evidence.period_fit: Civil nuclear exposure context relevant to 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-level nuclear infrastructure, not Bolsonaro personal control over weapons systems.
contrary_evidence: Civil reactors are not the same as an existential-risk weapons capability.
